lessons.title: Safety stock and service
lessons.question: What does a higher cycle service target cost?
lessons.mechanism: A higher target raises protection stock. Achieved unit fill rate is a different metric from the target cycle service level.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: A targets 90% CSL; B targets 99%. Neither is a promised fill rate.
lessons.reflect: Does the interval support a service gain? Which cost components changed, and why can achieved CSL differ from target?

lessons.title: Demand uncertainty
lessons.question: How does demand variability affect stock and shortages?
lessons.mechanism: CV scales demand dispersion, not just average volume. Nonnegative truncation can also alter the realised mean. Policies respond to configured uncertainty.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: Demand CV scale is 0.5 in A and 1.5 in B; shared seeds pair draws, not identical realised demand.
lessons.reflect: Inspect realised demand as well as fill rate. Is the effect stable with more replications?

lessons.title: Centralise or decentralise
lessons.question: Can stock pooling offset longer delivery lanes?
lessons.mechanism: Changing DC count changes locations, assignment, fixed costs, inventory and freight together. This is a network design comparison, not an isolated proof of risk pooling.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: Compare one DC with four under the same demand settings.
lessons.reflect: Separate fixed, freight, shortage and holding cost changes. What extra experiment would isolate demand correlation?

lessons.title: Forecast responsiveness
lessons.question: Does a smoother forecast improve replenishment?
lessons.mechanism: A shorter moving average responds faster but may amplify noise. Pre-demand forecasts are logged before observing that day; DCs observe order signals by default.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: Moving-average windows are 7 days in A and 28 days in B; both use forecasting.
lessons.reflect: Use the relationship chart for forecast versus demand. Compare SKU wMAPE and bias in diagnostics; does lower error guarantee lower cost?

lessons.title: Find the dispatch bottleneck
lessons.question: Where does a capacity cut first reduce customer service?
lessons.mechanism: DC capacity limits daily dispatch shared across SKUs. A constrained facility can hold inventory while downstream customers face shortages.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: B uses 35% of candidate DC dispatch capacity; A uses 100%.
lessons.reflect: Check facility utilization and retailer receipts. Is adding stock enough when dispatch throughput is constrained?

lessons.title: Supplier reliability
lessons.question: How do uncertain supplier delays propagate downstream?
lessons.mechanism: Supplier delays add to transit time on affected shipments. Inventory position includes outstanding orders, so more pipeline stock need not mean more stock on the shelf.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: S1 has no extra delay in A; B adds seven days with probability 0.5. Other supplier assumptions are inherited.
lessons.reflect: Trace S1 lanes and the ordering pipeline. Are all SKUs affected equally? Which mitigation would you test next?

lessons.title: Trace a supplier interruption
lessons.question: How long does downstream inventory protect service?
lessons.mechanism: An outage removes dispatch capacity. Existing in-transit shipments can still arrive, so service need not fail on the first event day.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: B removes all S1 capacity for days 120 to 140 inclusive; A has no event.
lessons.reflect: Compare receipts, on-order and backorders around the event. Distinguish first shortage from sustained recovery.

lessons.title: Protect service with a buffer
lessons.question: Is a seven-day buffer worth its holding cost?
lessons.mechanism: The buffer adds initial stock at non-supplier nodes. It is not an adaptive safety-stock optimisation; initial acquisition is excluded from the operating ledger.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: Both runs share the same S1 outage; B adds seven nominal-demand days of initial buffer.
lessons.reflect: Does buffer protection survive the warm-up? Include excluded initial acquisition before recommending a real investment.

lessons.title: Seasonal replenishment
lessons.question: Does the replenishment pipeline cope with seasonal peaks?
lessons.mechanism: Monthly multipliers alter the synthetic calendar demand. These indices are not normalised; volume and timing both change. Known-demand policies do not anticipate seasonal peaks.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: A uses a flat index of 1; B uses the documented synthetic twelve-month profile. Day zero is January 1 in the synthetic calendar.
lessons.reflect: Compare a full year, not only the first month. Repeat with equal annual-volume indices to isolate timing.

lessons.title: Backorders versus lost sales
lessons.question: What does the treatment of unfilled demand change?
lessons.mechanism: Backorders remain to be filled later; lost demand disappears. Immediate fill excludes later backlog clearance. A smaller backlog does not by itself mean better service.
lessons.assumption: ASSUMPTION: A backorders unfilled demand; B treats it as lost sales. Revenue and customer abandonment behaviour are not modelled.
lessons.reflect: Compare demand, immediate service and backlog. What commercial evidence would be needed to choose a real shortage policy?

daily_steps.title: Receive
daily_steps.text: Today’s arrivals enter stock and leave the in-transit pipeline.

daily_steps.title: Meet demand
daily_steps.text: Serve customer demand from stock; remaining demand becomes backlog or lost sales.

daily_steps.title: Update forecast
daily_steps.text: Observe demand/order signals and update the replenishment estimate after demand.

daily_steps.title: Review & order
daily_steps.text: Check inventory position, policy and review calendar; apply MOQ and pack rounding.

daily_steps.title: Dispatch
daily_steps.text: Allocate upstream inventory and capacity; schedule shipments with lane lead times.

daily_steps.title: Close the day
daily_steps.text: Log ending stock, pipeline and backlog; accrue operating costs.

glossary.definition: Immediate units served divided by units demanded. Zero-demand observations are unavailable, not zero service.
Fraction of completed measured replenishment cycles with no shortage. Target CSL is a policy input, not a guaranteed outcome.
On-hand plus on-order minus outstanding backlog; differs from physical on-hand stock.
Closing on-hand divided by the current planning demand estimate. No positive denominator means unavailable.
365 divided by annualised inventory turns; based on measured time-weighted inventory value. It is not daily cover.
Variance of weekly orders divided by variance of weekly customer demand. A zero demand variance leaves the ratio unavailable.
A 95% t interval for replication-level B minus A differences. An interval containing zero does not establish a direction.
The same seed streams pair experimental conditions. Changed demand or network assumptions can still change realised quantities.
Simulated days before measurement, intended to reduce initialization effects. Sufficiency must be checked; a default is not evidence.
Synthetic results describe this model under its assumptions. Validate units, parameters and held-out behaviour before real planning use.
